profile.address: Garden State Parkway, Wall Township, Monmouth County, New Jersey, 08720
profile.reading:
The Manasquan Cable Landing Station sits in Wall Township, Monmouth County, New Jersey, close to the Jersey Shore a few miles inland from Manasquan Inlet. Cable & Wireless USA built the station specifically to land its private Apollo submarine cable system, a transatlantic route connecting the United States to landing points in the United Kingdom and France. When Cable & Wireless's global network assets were folded into Vodafone, ownership of the Manasquan station transferred with them, and Vodafone operates the Apollo system's US landing infrastructure today.

Like other cable landing stations, this building's function is narrow and specific. It terminates the undersea fiber pairs, houses the submarine line terminating equipment and repeater power feed equipment, and connects Apollo's capacity into backhaul networks running toward New York and other inland hubs. It is carrier infrastructure, not a commercial colocation facility, and Vodafone does not publish square footage, power capacity, or customer tenancy figures for it, which is typical across the submarine cable industry.

Wall Township has become something of a cable landing hub in its own right. Tata Communications operates its own landing station in the township, and the NJFX carrier-neutral cable campus sits within a few miles, giving this corner of Monmouth County an unusual concentration of transatlantic connectivity infrastructure for a suburban New Jersey community.

reading.body:
Manasquan Cable Landing Station (Apollo) is a submarine cable terminus operated by Vodafone on the New Jersey coast, not a data center campus. It is one of two US landing points for the Apollo transatlantic fiber system, which connects onward to major data center hubs in New York City, Washington DC, and Ashburn, Virginia. No IT megawattage capacity is published, as would be expected for a cable landing station rather than a compute facility.

This facility functions as infrastructure for data center connectivity rather than as a host for compute itself. The published megawattage ranking shown in the state context does not apply to this site because it publishes no IT load figure. New Jersey has 48 mapped facilities in the registry, of which only five publish capacity; those five account for 111.3 MW total, but this cable station is not among the sources of that figure.

The site matters to AI infrastructure as a chokepoint for transatlantic data transit to and from major US data center regions, but not as a source of local compute capacity. Its strategic value lies in the submarine cable connectivity it provides to the hubs where AI training clusters are actually deployed. Whether this cable landing station represents a constraint on AI scaling depends on the total available transatlantic fiber bandwidth and utilization, neither of which is published here.
